title: Halt established Alzheimer’s disease and restore lost function

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that durably stops worsening in people who already have Alzheimer’s disease and restores meaningful lost cognitive abilities and everyday function. Disease arrest and functional recovery are separate goals: preventing further decline would not by itself demonstrate recovery, while a temporary improvement would not establish that the underlying disease had stopped.

Conceptual scope: the goal does not prescribe a particular mechanism or treatment schedule. A single upstream intervention, a combination addressing amyloid and tau, or treatment coupled with tissue or circuit repair are possible approaches raised in the supplied research, rather than established requirements. A continuing treatment could meet the clinical goal; a one-time cure would be a stronger claim requiring additional evidence.

significance.text: Conditional significance: durable arrest together with meaningful recovery would extend therapeutic capability to people for whom prevention has come too late. Its direct value would be demonstrated through regained abilities, greater independence and preservation of those gains. Reduced caregiving demands and broader social benefits would be downstream possibilities whose extent would depend on the magnitude, durability, safety and accessibility of the treatment.

Conceptual limit: stopping a damaging process and reconstructing what it has already destroyed are different accomplishments. Improvement through recovery of impaired surviving circuits would not establish replacement of lost neurons or restoration of every affected memory. If extensive neuronal loss constrains recovery, additional repair might be needed; the supplied evidence cannot establish when that would be necessary or whether it would be achievable. Success at one disease stage would not establish reversal at all stages.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed scientific challenge: identify interventions that both arrest the disease process in established illness and permit sustained functional recovery. The research frames the problem as interacting pathology, synaptic dysfunction and neuronal loss, but those premises are not documented in inspectable scientific content in the supplied evidence. Within that working model, key questions are which processes remain causal at each stage, which must be changed together, and which impairments remain reversible.

Proposed engineering and translational barriers include reaching the relevant cells and circuits safely, achieving an adequate and durable biological effect, and connecting that effect to clinical benefit. If recovery requires tissue or circuit reconstruction, restoring useful integration while preserving learned information adds a separate challenge. None of these possibilities establishes that clearance of a particular protein, brain-wide delivery or tissue replacement is universally necessary.

Proposed measurement challenge: distinguish biological target engagement, temporary symptom relief, durable arrest and recovery of lost function. A change in a molecular measurement addresses a different question from whether a person regains reliable memory or daily living abilities. Establishing the breakthrough therefore requires clinical outcomes alongside mechanistic measurements, with disease stage, baseline impairment and treatment exposure defined clearly.

current_state.text: The supplied bibliographic record identifies a study attributed to Mummery and colleagues, dated 24 April 2023, titled “Tau-targeting antisense oligonucleotide MAPTRx in mild Alzheimer’s disease: a phase 1b, randomized, placebo-controlled trial,” with DOI 10.1038/s41591-023-02326-3. However, the validated review reports that the retained HTML contains only a cookie-access message. The document’s identity, abstract and scientific results could not be verified from that retained content.

The earlier research describes this as a randomized phase Ib study in mild Alzheimer’s disease, primarily designed to assess safety, with dose-dependent reductions in cerebrospinal-fluid total tau and reductions in higher-dose groups. These remain attributed reports from the supplied research: the available artifact does not permit checking the design, population, dose response, safety objective or results. No numerical reduction, sample size or follow-up duration is supplied. The earlier statement that the abstract was inspected cannot be retained as verified.

Even if the reported tau reductions are accurate, a biomarker response alone would not demonstrate durable disease arrest, restored cognition or improved daily function. The supplied material establishes no such revolutionary clinical outcome. The access barrier leaves the reported study findings unresolved in this record; it is not evidence that those findings are false.

Coverage limitation: the supplied freshness record is empty. This record therefore cannot establish comprehensive coverage through 1 November 2026 or determine the field’s present status. That limitation is separate from the accuracy of the dated 2023 study description and does not invalidate a result merely because it is older.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: replicated controlled trials in clearly defined established Alzheimer’s disease should show both durable arrest of progression and meaningful improvement in independently assessed cognition and daily function, with acceptable safety. Protocols should specify disease stage, baseline impairment, what counts as arrest, the magnitude of clinically meaningful recovery and the follow-up interval before results are known. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated controlled trials demonstrate durable arrest and meaningful functional recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidentiary design: clinical assessments should distinguish regained abilities from transient symptomatic effects, repeated-testing effects and changes confined to a biomarker. Mechanistic measurements should establish which targets the intervention changes, while clinical endpoints establish whether those changes help patients. Independent replication and consistent findings across relevant patient groups would strengthen confidence; finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth rather than effectiveness for every patient or stage.
completion_criteria.label: Clinical assessments distinguish recovery from symptomatic effects and testing artifacts

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and practical boundaries: report whether benefits require continuing treatment, how long they persist, adverse effects, treatment burden and the populations for which recovery remains limited. A claim of a one-time cure would require sufficiently long observation without continuing treatment to support sustained arrest and recovery. The supplied material does not determine a sufficient duration, an acceptable safety threshold or a numerical minimum for meaningful benefit.
completion_criteria.label: Report benefit durability, treatment requirements and practical limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-09, “Prevent Alzheimer’s dementia before irreversible functional loss,” shares the disease focus but addresses an earlier intervention window. NRL-11 requires benefit after impairment is established and explicitly includes recovery of lost function. Prevention success would not by itself demonstrate this capability, and success in established disease would not establish the best preventive approach.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-04, “Read and selectively repair the physical traces of specific memories,” concerns targeted memory repair; NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” concerns reconstruction that retains learned abilities. Either could overlap with recovery in advanced Alzheimer’s disease, depending on what limits reversibility. NRL-11 could also succeed through restoration of surviving circuits without achieving either broader capability.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” could enable some molecular or regenerative treatments, but delivery alone would not establish disease arrest or functional recovery. NRL-15, “Identify and treat shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration across diseases,” could supply relevant mechanisms; success in Alzheimer’s disease would still require disease-specific clinical evidence and would not establish efficacy across other neurodegenerative conditions.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation,” and NRL-03, “Whole-brain, cellular-resolution recording during natural behavior,” could help explain or measure circuit dysfunction and recovery. They remain distinct theoretical and measurement goals. Neither capability is established here as a prerequisite for a successful Alzheimer’s treatment.

brief.title: An end to Alzheimer’s decline and recovery of lost abilities
possible: People who already have Alzheimer’s disease could regain meaningful memory, thinking skills and everyday abilities while the disease stops worsening. Treatment would preserve those gains over time.
why: People whose abilities have already declined could regain independence. Families and caregivers could face fewer demands as people recover the ability to manage daily life.

sources.showed: A small safety trial tested MAPTRx, a drug targeting tau, a protein linked to Alzheimer’s damage. Treatment lowered tau in the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
sources.quote: Evaluation of a tau-targeting antisense oligonucleotide in a phase 1 trial of patients with mild AD found it was well tolerated and resulted in a sustained reduction of tau protein levels.
sources.cited_for: Treatment can lower tau in people with mild Alzheimer’s disease.
sources.not_established: Lower tau levels alone do not establish lasting disease arrest or recovery of everyday abilities.

sources.who: Christopher H. van Dyck and colleagues
sources.showed: Lecanemab reduced amyloid, a protein that accumulates in Alzheimer’s disease, and slowed decline in thinking and daily function in early disease.
sources.quote:
there were greater reductions in brain amyloid burden with lecanemab 
than with placebo
sources.cited_for: A treatment targeting amyloid can slow clinical decline.
sources.not_established: Participants continued to decline, and the trial did not demonstrate recovery of lost abilities.

sources.showed: A small, short trial of intensive diet, exercise, stress management and group support reported improvement on some thinking and function measures in early Alzheimer’s disease.
sources.quote: CGIC, CDR Global, and ADAS-Cog showed improvement in cognition and function and CDR-SB showed significantly less progression, compared to the control group which worsened in all four measures.
sources.cited_for: Intensive lifestyle changes produced short-term signs of improvement in early disease.
sources.not_established: This small trial does not establish replicated, durable disease arrest and meaningful recovery.

sources.who: Jennifer A Zimmer and colleagues at Eli Lilly and Company
sources.showed: Donanemab slowed decline over 3 years in early Alzheimer’s disease, including after some participants completed treatment. Longer-term comparisons included an external patient group.
sources.quote: No new safety signals were observed compared to the established donanemab safety profile.
sources.cited_for: Slower decline can persist after a limited course of treatment.
sources.not_established: The study demonstrated slower progression, while sustained arrest and recovery remain unproven.

shown: Van Dyck and colleagues showed slower decline with lecanemab in early Alzheimer’s disease. Zimmer and colleagues reported continued slowing with donanemab after some participants finished treatment.
Ornish and colleagues reported improvements on some thinking and function measures after 20 weeks of intensive lifestyle changes. The trial was small, and lasting recovery remains unproven.
missing: Repeated controlled trials have yet to demonstrate lasting disease arrest together with meaningful recovery of thinking and everyday abilities.
Clinical assessments must establish that regained abilities persist beyond temporary symptom relief or improvements from repeated testing.
Long-term studies must establish safety, treatment burden and whether maintaining recovered abilities requires continuing treatment.

milestones.label: Repeated trials demonstrate lasting arrest and meaningful recovery
milestones.explanation: Repeated controlled trials would have to show sustained disease arrest and independently assessed gains in thinking and daily function, with acceptable safety. This would establish lasting benefit in defined stages of Alzheimer’s disease.

milestones.label: Assessments establish genuine recovery of lost abilities
milestones.explanation: Assessments would have to distinguish regained abilities from temporary symptom relief, repeated-testing effects and molecular changes. This would establish that treatment helps people recover useful function.

milestones.label: Benefits, treatment needs and practical limits become clear
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to establish how long gains last, ongoing treatment needs, harms, burden and limits across patient groups. This would define the conditions under which recovery can be maintained.

uncertain: How much lost function remains recoverable at different disease stages, and when would rebuilding brain tissue or connections be necessary?
How much recovery, how long a follow-up and what level of risk would justify a claim of lasting arrest and recovery?

page.title: Disease arrest and functional recovery in Alzheimer’s disease
page.definition: A treatment stops further clinical progression in people with symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease and restores lost cognition and everyday abilities, such as paying bills or dressing. The gains persist over a defined period and reflect a change in disease course. In the closest established clinical example, people with early Alzheimer’s who received lecanemab declined more slowly on average over 18 months.

goal.need: An estimated 7.4 million Americans aged 65 or older have clinical Alzheimer’s dementia in 2026. In 2025, unpaid caregivers provided 19.6 billion hours of help to Americans with Alzheimer’s or other dementias. Medicines that slow early Alzheimer’s can give people more time at their current level of ability. Someone who already needs help shopping or dressing could do more independently if those abilities returned and lasted. The scope for recovery is less certain once brain damage is severe.

completion.title: Controlled clinical evidence establishes sustained disease arrest and cognitive and functional recovery.
completion.criterion: Controlled clinical evidence in a defined population with biomarker-confirmed symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease demonstrates both cessation of clinical progression and clinically meaningful gains from impaired baseline in cognition and everyday function, maintained over prespecified follow-up. Evidence distinguishes changed disease course from symptomatic benefit. Arrest margins, recovery thresholds and observation duration are justified for that population; no universal numerical values were found.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; no outside body’s combined arrest-and-recovery test was found.
completion.basis: Regulatory guidance addresses clinical benefit and evidence of a change in disease course. The combined test requires positive evidence of arrest as well as sustained recovery in both domains. A nonsignificant test for worsening leaves the magnitude of possible decline unresolved. The external counterpulsation trial illustrates the distinction: it reported gains in cognition and daily activities in clinically diagnosed patients and left open whether treatment altered the underlying disease.

milestones.title: Nonclinical studies support first human exposure to an Alzheimer’s treatment.
milestones.criterion: Pharmacology and toxicology studies in animals or in vitro provide adequate information for the sponsor to conclude that the proposed first human investigation is reasonably safe. The nature and duration of that investigation determine the scope of testing.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8); a general investigational-drug requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: Human studies establish exposure and tolerability sufficient for phase 2 Alzheimer’s testing.
milestones.criterion: Human studies characterize tolerability, drug exposure and pharmacological effects sufficiently to design a well-controlled phase 2 study.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Phase 1 IND Frequently Asked Questions, question 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: information about the drug's pharmacokinetics and pharmacological effects should be obtained to permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies.

milestones.title: A phase 3 trial shows less decline on a combined clinical scale at 18 months in early Alzheimer’s.
milestones.criterion: In participants with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer’s and confirmed amyloid pathology, treatment produces less mean worsening than placebo from baseline to 18 months on the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes. The score combines cognition and everyday function and ranges from 0 to 18, with higher scores indicating greater impairment. The superiority test uses a two-sided significance level of 0.05.
milestones.set_by: Eisai and the Clarity AD investigators, NCT03887455 protocol as described in the trial publication; this endpoint concerns early Alzheimer’s disease.
milestones.threshold_quote: change from baseline at 18 months in the score on the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes

milestones.title: An Alzheimer’s treatment preserves an early-start clinical advantage after delayed treatment begins.
milestones.criterion: After the delayed-start group begins treatment, the early-start group retains its advantage on the clinical measures throughout the delayed-start phase. Follow-up and analysis must be sufficient to distinguish a maintained difference from two trajectories that are still converging.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, CHMP guideline CPMP/EWP/553/95 Rev.2, section 8.3.2; a proposed demonstration of disease modification.
milestones.threshold_quote: the difference in clinical measures between delayed-start patients and those who started treatment early is maintained throughout the study.

milestones.title: A controlled Alzheimer’s trial demonstrates sustained recovery of cognition and everyday function.
milestones.criterion: A controlled study shows a treatment benefit over the comparison group and clinically meaningful improvement from the treated group’s own impaired baseline in both cognition and everyday function. The gains in both domains persist over prespecified follow-up.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; searches of FDA and EMA guidance and recovery-trial endpoints found no established magnitude-and-duration test for sustained recovery in both domains.

milestones.title: Treatment reduces established brain pathology below its pretreatment level in an animal model.
milestones.criterion: In an animal model of Alzheimer-related pathology, document the lesion burden when treatment begins. Show that the burden falls below that starting level after treatment, using a baseline cohort or serial measurements and an appropriate comparison group. A lower endpoint burden than in untreated animals can also arise from slower accumulation.
milestones.set_by: Expert advisory panel convened by the Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation, Charles River Discovery Services and Cerebricon, 2011 recommendations on preclinical animal studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: whether the treatment reduced pre-existing pathology in the brain or simply slowed its age-associated accumulation.

milestones.title: Phase 2b shows at least an 80% probability of 25% less clinical decline at 12 months.
milestones.criterion: In early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, the prespecified Bayesian analysis gives at least an 80% probability of at least 25% less decline than placebo on the Alzheimer’s Disease Composite Score at 12 months. Apply the test to the simplest dosing regimen estimated to achieve at least 90% of the maximum treatment effect.
milestones.set_by: Eisai and the Study 201 investigators, registered phase 2b protocol NCT01767311. The probability and effect-size thresholds are specific to this trial.
milestones.threshold_quote: an 80% probability that the ED90 dose achieved at least 25% less clinical decline compared to placebo on ADCOMS.

milestones.title: Controlled follow-up establishes arrest of clinical progression in symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease.
milestones.criterion: In a defined population with biomarker-confirmed symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, repeated clinical assessments show a treatment benefit over control and rule out continued worsening in the treated group greater than a prespecified, clinically justified arrest margin over a prespecified period. Justify the margin and duration for the population and measures used.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas. EMA names arrest as a goal. No outside body was found to specify a clinical arrest margin and observation period for this test.

not_found: No published combined arrest-and-recovery criterion specifying recovery magnitude, arrest margin and sufficient observation duration was found.

results.finding: In lecanemab-treated Clarity AD participants with no/low tau (subgroup n unreported), 61% improved on cognition at month 36.
results.detail: The subgroup analysis was exploratory. The recovery percentages came from open-label follow-up and were reported separately for the two scales.
results.quote: Similar results were observed for ADAS‐Cog14 (63% and 61% in no/low tau PET and 46% and 43% for low amyloid) and ADCS MCI‐ADL (63% and 59% in no/low tau PET and 51% and 48% for low amyloid).

results.finding: In clinically diagnosed early Alzheimer’s disease (n=190), full-pressure counterpulsation improved mean ADCS-ADL by 1.6 points from baseline at one year.
results.detail: The groups received six months of treatment followed by observation. ADCS-ADL assessors were blinded, while VADAS-cog assessors were not guaranteed to be blinded. The joint outcome grouped improvement with stability.
results.quote: Improvement over baseline persisted through the 1-year assessment at which time gain from baseline in the full-pressure treatment participants was 1.6 (95% CI: 0.01 – 3.19) compared to the low-pressure group which had declined at -2.8 (95% CI: -5.59 – -0.01), p=0.007.

results.finding: In clinically diagnosed early Alzheimer’s disease (n=190), 57% of the full-pressure arm improved or remained stable in both cognition and function at one year.
results.detail: The study assessed change from baseline and superiority over low-pressure treatment. It did not estimate an arrest margin or justify a follow-up duration for testing arrest.
results.quote: Further, at the 1-year assessment, 57% of full-pressure ECP patients had either improved over baseline or remained stable in  both  cognition and function (VADAS-cog and ADCS-ADL).

results.finding: In amyloid-confirmed early Alzheimer’s disease (N=1,795 randomized), lecanemab showed less CDR-SB worsening than placebo at 18 months.
results.detail: Figure 3 presents the CDR-SB trajectories. The paper refers readers to the prior publication for the primary core analysis.

results.finding: Among lecanemab recipients (N=1,616), the early-start group retained its observed CDR-SB advantage through month 36.
results.detail: The duration describes follow-up from core baseline. The extension analyses used no formal hypothesis testing.
results.quote: Separation between early and delayed start was maintained between 18 and 36 months.

results.finding: In the lecanemab no/low tau PET subgroup (N unreported), 59% had no CDR-SB worsening from baseline at month 36.
results.detail: The 59% is an exploratory responder proportion at one visit. The paper reports 1,616 lecanemab recipients overall.
results.quote: with 59% having no decline and 51% having improvement at 36 months in the no/low tau PET subgroup

results.finding: In the lecanemab no/low tau PET subgroup (N unreported), 59% improved from baseline on the everyday-function scale at month 36.
results.detail: The subgroup analysis was exploratory. During the extension, both the early-start and delayed-start groups received lecanemab.
results.quote: Similar results were observed for ADAS‐Cog14 (63% and 61% in no/low tau PET and 46% and 43% for low amyloid) and ADCS MCI‐ADL (63% and 59% in no/low tau PET and 51% and 48% for low amyloid).

results.finding: AL002 had a no-observed-adverse-effect level of 250 mg/kg in a repeat-dose toxicology study of 32 cynomolgus monkeys.
results.detail: Minimal unilateral microscopic changes in the ocular ciliary body at the highest dose were judged nonadverse.
results.quote:
IV administration of 
AL002 at doses up to 250 mg/kg weekly for 4 weeks was 
well tolerated, with no AL002-related adverse effects on 
any measured safety parameter.

results.finding: Lecanemab (sample size unspecified): FDA issued a Study May Proceed Letter for first human exposure in 2010.
results.detail: The milestone is supported by the IND regulatory history on page 11. The later marketing application reviewed a broader nonclinical package.
results.quote:
A Study May Proceed Letter was issued to the applicant on 
October 27, 2010.

results.finding: In the donanemab Alzheimer’s phase 1b trial (N=61), 50% of the 10 participants in the highest repeat-dose cohort achieved PET-defined amyloid clearance.
results.detail: The highest repeat-dose cohort received 20 mg/kg intravenously every four weeks. Clearance was defined by a 24.1-Centiloid PET threshold.
results.quote: Furthermore, complete amyloid clearance, as measured by florbetapir PET, was observed for 5 of 10 patients (50.0%) treated with 20-mg/ kg Q4W donanemab.

results.finding: In mild Alzheimer’s disease (n=1,322 randomized), early-start solanezumab met noninferiority for preserving its cognitive and functional advantage through week 132.
results.detail: Week 132 was 52 weeks after crossover. At the final visit, both estimates still favored early initiation, but neither difference was statistically significant. Only 43% of delayed-start and 45% of early-start patients completed the full analysis period.

results.finding: Among 256 Alzheimer’s patients receiving rivastigmine capsules, 28% showed sustained improvement in each domain when assessed separately.
results.detail: The paper cites a 4-point cognitive responder threshold and gives no corresponding clinical meaningfulness threshold for everyday function. The two 28% rates do not establish how many patients improved in both domains.
results.quote: Sustained improvements of 4 or 5 points on the ADAS-cog or ADCS-ADL were demonstrated in the 9.5-mg/24-h rivastigmine patch (24% and 36% of patients, respectively) and 12-mg/d capsule groups (28% on both outcome measures).

results.finding: PS19 tauopathy mice given a tau-targeting ASO (n=6) had lower whole-brain AT8-positive tau burden than the pretreatment cohort (p=0.011).
results.quote: Following reduction of human tau in this mouse model of tauopathy, fewer tau inclusions developed and pre-existing phosphorylated tau and thioflavin S pathology was reversed.

results.finding: Phase 2b lecanemab in early Alzheimer’s (854 treated): 63.8% probability of at least 25% less ADCOMS decline than placebo at 12 months.
results.detail: Table 2 lists 143 participants for the ED90 arm and 229 for placebo in the 12-month analysis. The abstract rounds the probability to 64%.
results.quote:
At 12 months, the 10-mg/
kg biweekly ED90 dose showed a 64% probability to be better than placebo by 25% on ADCOMS, which missed
the 80% threshold for the primary outcome.

results.finding: In 50 randomized patients with biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer’s dementia, precuneus rTMS yielded an estimated 0.25-point CDR-SB worsening by week 24.
results.detail: The paper cites a 1–2-point clinically important increase and uses a ≤1-point change to classify responders. The analysis did not test whether treated-group worsening stayed below a prespecified arrest margin.
results.quote:
The GLMM 
estimated mean change (W0−W24) in CDR-SB score was −0.25 for 
PC-rTMS [95% confidence interval (CI) (−4.8, 4.3)] and −1.42 for 
sham-rTMS group [95% CI (−6.0, 3.3)] (Fig. 3A ).

definition = "A treatment stops further clinical progression in people with symptomatic Alzheimer\u2019s disease and restores lost cognition and everyday abilities, such as paying bills or dressing. The gains persist over a defined period and reflect a change in disease course. In the closest established clinical example, people with early Alzheimer\u2019s who received lecanemab declined more slowly on average over 18 months.". Reason: The definition leaves everyday function abstract and omits the clinical distinction between recovery and the slowing already demonstrated in early disease.

goal.need = "An estimated 7.4 million Americans aged 65 or older have clinical Alzheimer\u2019s dementia in 2026. In 2025, unpaid caregivers provided 19.6 billion hours of help to Americans with Alzheimer\u2019s or other dementias. Medicines that slow early Alzheimer\u2019s can give people more time at their current level of ability. Someone who already needs help shopping or dressing could do more independently if those abilities returned and lasted. The scope for recovery is less certain once brain damage is severe.". Reason: The current rationale gives the scale of caregiving but leaves unexplained what recovery would change for a person who already needs help.

add statement by European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2018: "slowing or arrest of symptom progression". Reason: EMA’s guideline explicitly names arrest as a treatment goal and separately identifies improvement in cognition and function.

edit completion: basis = "Regulatory guidance addresses clinical benefit and evidence of a change in disease course. The combined test requires positive evidence of arrest as well as sustained recovery in both domains. A nonsignificant test for worsening leaves the magnitude of possible decline unresolved. The external counterpulsation trial illustrates the distinction: it reported gains in cognition and daily activities in clinically diagnosed patients and left open whether treatment altered the underlying disease."; refs = [2, 3, 4, 5, 14]. Reason: The basis should explain how a controlled trial can report recovery in both domains while leaving disease arrest unresolved.

add milestone after None: "Treatment reduces established brain pathology below its pretreatment level in an animal model.". Reason: Direct evidence that treatment reverses established pathology in an animal model is a laboratory result distinct from the safety assessment for human exposure.

edit m1: criterion = "Pharmacology and toxicology studies in animals or in vitro provide adequate information for the sponsor to conclude that the proposed first human investigation is reasonably safe. The nature and duration of that investigation determine the scope of testing."; refs = [6]. Reason: The mouse efficacy result embedded in the criterion does not establish the toxicological safety of first human exposure.

edit m2: criterion = "Human studies characterize tolerability, drug exposure and pharmacological effects sufficiently to design a well-controlled phase 2 study."; refs = [8, 9]. Reason: The MAPTRx adverse-event rates and tau measurements are observations from one trial and obscure the phase 1 decision the milestone tests.

add milestone after m2: "Phase 2b shows at least an 80% probability of 25% less clinical decline at 12 months.". Reason: The entry jumps from readiness for phase 2 to phase 3 efficacy without a clinical proof-of-concept test.

edit m3: title = "A phase 3 trial shows less decline on a combined clinical scale at 18 months in early Alzheimer\u2019s."; criterion = "In participants with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer\u2019s and confirmed amyloid pathology, treatment produces less mean worsening than placebo from baseline to 18 months on the Clinical Dementia Rating\u2013Sum of Boxes. The score combines cognition and everyday function and ranges from 0 to 18, with higher scores indicating greater impairment. The superiority test uses a two-sided significance level of 0.05."; threshold_quote = "change from baseline at 18 months in the score on the Clinical Dementia Rating\u2013Sum of Boxes"; threshold_ref = 10; refs = [10]. Reason: Clarity AD tested a combined score in early disease, and the current title can be read as requiring separate demonstrations in cognition and function at any disease stage.

edit m4: criterion = "After the delayed-start group begins treatment, the early-start group retains its advantage on the clinical measures throughout the delayed-start phase. Follow-up and analysis must be sufficient to distinguish a maintained difference from two trajectories that are still converging."; refs = [5, 11]. Reason: The extension’s hazard ratio measures progression to another clinical stage, whereas the delayed-start test asks whether the original clinical advantage persists throughout follow-up.

add milestone after m4: "Controlled follow-up establishes arrest of clinical progression in symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease.". Reason: Sustained cessation of clinical progression is a distinct component of completion that neither slower decline nor a lasting early-start advantage establishes.

edit m5: criterion = "A controlled study shows a treatment benefit over the comparison group and clinically meaningful improvement from the treated group\u2019s own impaired baseline in both cognition and everyday function. The gains in both domains persist over prespecified follow-up."; refs = [2, 4, 5, 12, 14]. Reason: The lifestyle trial’s global ratings and cognitive comparison are results to judge, while the criterion needs to identify the baseline, comparator and domains required for recovery.
